summary: Terrain Mapper finds places on Earth whose 3D terrain shape matches a chosen area of the Moon. A researcher picks a lunar target and says what they want to test: rover mobility, navigation, communications line of sight or astronaut traverses. They also say how far along their project is. The tool compares 32 km elevation patches using three measures of shape: the cross-section of the main landform, the surface texture and roughness, and the size of the relief. It ranks Earth sites by how well they match, how easy they are to reach, how often they can be used and how much they cost. It shows the target and each match side by side in 3D. A Discover button searches bare ground across the whole planet for new candidate sites beyond the well-known analogue list. Testing on Earth is cheaper and safer than testing on the Moon, so finding the right ground early saves missions time and money. This is a test version with a limited dataset: three Moon targets, 19 Earth regions and 553 extra patches at 500 m resolution. The 3D matches still need checking against higher-resolution data and by people who know these sites before anyone plans fieldwork around them.
details:
• The tool cuts every site into 64 × 64 elevation grids at 500 m spacing and subtracts each patch’s median height, so only the shape is compared.
    1. Profile: the average cross-section across the main landform, compared with derivative dynamic time warping. A ridge reads the same at any angle.
    2. Texture: ruggedness, surface area ratio, short- and long-range roughness and the Hurst exponent, compared with Mahalanobis distance.
    3. Magnitude: how tall the relief is and how steep the steepest slopes are.
  • Each score becomes a percentile against all Earth patches. They’re combined with a geometric mean with no hand-set weights, so the result shows which part of the match is weakest.
  • A confidence flag (known, edge or novel) says whether Earth has anything genuinely close to the target.
  • Results show fidelity, accessibility, repeatability and affordability, a radar chart, a Pareto badge and synced 3D views of the target and the match.
  • A Map page shows every site, and a Discover page ranks bare-ground patches from beyond the known analogue sites.

Factors I considered

Fidelity, Verification methods, The limited dataset using only 3 moon targets, and the cost of running experiments.

  1. Data honesty. Every value carries its source. Curated costs, seasons and permits stay blank until filled from the ESA catalogue, and the app shows them as unknown.
    • This is a test with three Moon targets, 19 Earth regions and 553 Discover patches at 500 m.
    • Rover-scale rocks, regolith, gravity and temperature fall outside its scope.
    • Mars targets are paused because the Mars elevation service returned flat data.
  2. Bare terrain. The Earth elevation model includes trees and buildings, so we used desert, volcanic and polar sites and filtered Discover with land-cover data.
  3. Access, cost and permits. Places like Antarctica match well but are expensive and permit-heavy. The scores make that visible.
  4. Lightweight running. All heavy processing happens ahead of time, so searches finish in under half a second online.
